rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality occurs in both states because the indices wrap modulo 17.

Initially, head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, and count_ = 0: the queue is empty, so pop returns false. After pushing values 0 through 16, head_ = 0, tail_ = 0, and count_ = 17: the queue is full, so another push returns false without changing anything.

The implementation distinguishes them using count_: empty means count_ == 0, and full means count_ == capacity. Its invariant is 0 ≤ count_ ≤ 17 and tail_ == (head_ + count_) % 17.

review.usefulPrefix: Index equality occurs in both states because the indices wrap modulo 17.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
Assuming IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, the original triple gives 1 in both parenthesizations; the changed triple gives 0 and 1.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + -16777216) + 1: cancellation gives exactly 0, then exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1): the inner result is -16777215, which is exactly representable. Adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + -16777216: the exact inner sum, 16777217, lies halfway between the representable values 16777216 and 16777218. Ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216, so the final cancellation gives 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + -16777216): the inner result is exactly representable as -16777215, so the final sum is exactly 1.

The key is the spacing boundary at 2²⁴: representable integers immediately below it are spaced by 1, while those immediately above it are spaced by 2. Thus -16777215 is representable, but 16777217 is not. A different rounding mode can change the rounded result of 16777216 + 1.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a new value can be observed and then disappear from a later read.

Start with version 0 on all five replicas. Use this fully ordered execution:
1. Invoke a write W of version 1.
2. Deliver W only to A. A stores 1 and acknowledges; W remains incomplete with just one acknowledgement.
3. Invoke read R1. Its queries return A:1, B:0, C:0. R1 returns 1.
4. After R1 finishes, invoke read R2. Its queries return B:0, D:0, E:0. R2 returns 0.
5. Leave W pending; no other writes occur.

To explain R1 returning 1, any attempted linearization must include the pending W and place it before R1. Because the reads do not overlap, real-time order requires R1 before R2. Thus the order must be W, R1, R2, and R2 must return 1—not 0. Omitting W instead makes R1’s result impossible. Either way, there is a contradiction.

Writing the selected version to three replicas and waiting for their acknowledgements before returning fixes this counterexample. For example, R1 propagates version 1 to A, B, C before finishing. Every subsequent three-replica read intersects those three in at least one replica, since 3 + 3 > 5. Replicas never decrease their versions, so R2 must observe version 1 or higher and cannot return 0. W can now be linearized before R1, despite remaining incomplete.

This is the quorum read-repair principle used for atomic registers. A general linearizability guarantee also requires a correct version-assignment protocol: versions must uniquely order writes and respect real-time precedence. The stated quorum rules alone do not specify that, especially for multiple writers.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires the first read to precede the second in the sequential history. If the first returns version 1 from the pending write, that write must be included and placed before the first read; with no intervening write, the second read cannot then return version 0.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Pending operations may be omitted or assigned a completion when constructing a linearization, but this particular write cannot be omitted because its value was returned by a completed read.

review.usefulPrefix: Because the first read completed before the second read began, linearizability requires the first read to precede the second in the sequential history.
